newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mayors discuss urban problems.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mayors discuss urban problems.

text.p: America's mayors met Saturday to discuss problems and opportunities facing the nation's cities, such as combatting drugs, raising the quality of education and improving transportation links.
More than 300 mayors attending the annual meeting of the U.S. Conference of Mayors held their formal opening session Saturday after a day of forums and workshops Friday.
Chicago Mayor Richard Daley, outgoing president of the conference, said the most important role mayors could play in reforming welfare and creating new jobs was to fix public schools.

"All across the nation, families of all racial groups and financial backgrounds are leaving cities because they have lost faith in urban public education," he said. "Improving schools is the only way to make a lasting change in this country."

Daley said that, in the past year, he had been inspired by a change in attitudes about public schools. "You don't see as many stories today about how test scores are falling year after year ... Instead there are more and more stories about schools that work," he said.
Daley said that, for too long, local governments had had to devote their energies to fighting the drug war "even though those drugs are not grown or produced in our cities."
There had been some encouraging signs in the past year and the mayors had to keep up the pressure, he said.

"We need to demand action from the federal government, getting federal agencies to use their full power to stop drug smuggling and money laundering. We need more federal cooperation with local law enforcement agencies," he said.
President Clinton is scheduled to speak Monday at the meeting, which lasts until Tuesday.
San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown talked about the recent narrow approval by the city's voters of a new football stadium.

"We as mayors literally have to find a way for entrepreneurship to occur in our communities. And we've got to do so because the state and the feds are no longer going to be in a position or willing to supply the resources that they supplied years ago. Yet the demand for services is going to be just as high," Brown told the conference.

U.S. Secretary of Transportation Rodney Slater stressed the importance of good transportation links to help move people from welfare to work. "Only six percent of all welfare recipients have cars ... All too many of them need transit to get them to jobs that are beyond the reach of our transit system," he said.

"We have businesses today that are literally crying out for capable and dedicated workers, but we need a transportation system to tie those people ... to the job opportunities, wherever those job opportunities are to be found," he said.
Amtrak Chief Executive Officer Thomas Downs sounded a warning about the future of the passenger railroad and urged the mayors to support the creation of a capital trust fund for Amtrak.
"This year, the Congress has to decide whether or not there is going to be an Amtrak in America's future," Downs said.
"We have said to the Congress that without a trust fund or some dedicated capital funding this railroad as we know it would cease to exist," he said.
He urged the mayors to support bills before Congress that would create a five-year capital trust fund for Amtrak.
